inline.s: Q: Why, in the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sutra, did the Buddha say: “Today what the Tathāgata calls the true self is called Buddha-nature.”?

A: Here “true self” is spoken in contrast to this false self of the five aggregates, body and mind. In the tenth chapter, “The Entrustment,” the Sixth Patriarch said: “Only recognize your own original mind; see your own original nature as neither moving nor still, neither arising nor ceasing.” And the meaning of “neither arising nor ceasing” is that it never existed to begin with, just as the Sixth Patriarch explained “neither arising nor ceasing” in the ninth chapter, “The Dharma-Protector”: “Originally there was never arising, and now there is also no ceasing.” In the Sutra on the Buddha’s Treasury, the Buddha said: “All dharmas neither arise nor cease, are without mark and without doing.” This shows that the original nature (that is, the tathāgatagarbha, the Buddha-nature) is also an illusion.
Q: If this is so, is the dharma body also an illusion?

A: The Sutra on the Contemplation of the Mind-Ground of the Great Vehicle says: “Always contemplate the wondrous dharma body of the Buddhas; its essence, like space, is unobtainable.” The Laṅkāvatāra Sutra of the Great Vehicle says: “The dharma body is like an illusion or a dream; how can it be praised? Knowing it as without self-nature and without arising — this is called praising the Buddha.”
Q: Then who is bound? Who creates karma? Who transmigrates? Who is liberated? And to where is one liberated?

A: Self-nature is bound, self-nature creates karma, self-nature transmigrates, self-nature is liberated. There are two stages to liberation: if one ends the birth-and-death of the delimited portions, one leaves the cycle and escapes the three realms; if one ends the birth-and-death of transformation, one perfectly realizes the Buddha fruit. As for where one is liberated to, according to the levels of liberation there are four lands to dwell in: the land where ordinary and holy dwell together, the land of remaining residue with expedient means, the land of real reward and adornment, and the land of eternal stillness and light. The land where ordinary and holy dwell together is the land where ordinary people and sages who manifest bodies and preach the Dharma to transform sentient beings dwell together; the land of remaining residue with expedient means is the land where the two vehicles and bodhisattvas who have not realized the dharma body dwell; the land of real reward and adornment is the land where the Buddha’s reward body and the bodhisattvas on the grounds dwell; the land of eternal stillness and light is the land where the Tathāgata’s pure dharma body abides in quiescence. These four lands are all matters within the dream of ignorance; a higher-level self-nature can go to a lower-level land, but a lower-level self-nature cannot go to a higher-level land. After becoming a Buddha, one may either remain in the dream of ignorance to transform sentient beings, or enter extinction; then that dreamer no longer dreams the dream of ignorance. (Regarding self-nature, see
The Mind, Self-Nature, and the Tathāgatagarbha
Q: The phrase “not mind, not Buddha, not a thing” — what does it mean?
Answer:
The Compendium of the Five Lamps records:
A monk asked: “Why does the master say that the mind is the Buddha?” The master
(Mazu)
said: “To stop the child’s crying
(this is an expedient saying for beginning students)

. The monk asked: “When the crying stops, what then?” The master said: “Not mind, not Buddha.” The monk asked: “Apart from these two kinds of people, how do you point them out?” The master said: “To him
(that one)
say: not a thing.”
The Compendium of the Five Lamps also says:

The Chan master Zizai of Funiu Mountain at Yique, a son of the Li clan of Wuxing. At first he followed the Chan master Guoyi, and after receiving the full precepts he studied with Mazu and awakened his mind-ground
(awakening)
. The master Mazu had him deliver a letter to the National Teacher Zhong
(the National Teacher Huizhong)
. The National Teacher asked: “With what Dharma does Master Ma instruct his disciples?” He said: “The mind is the Buddha.” The National Teacher said: “What kind of talk is that
(strongly disapproving)
!” After a long while
(after a long time)

he asked again: “Is there any further teaching besides this?” The master said: “Not mind, not Buddha. Or one might say: not mind, not Buddha, not a thing.” The National Teacher said: “That is somewhat better
(this is more or less right)

[To stop the child’s crying] A metaphor for expedient teaching (not ultimate teaching). When a child cries, an adult gives him a yellow poplar leaf, saying: “This is a gold piece; you can take it and buy candy.” The child, holding it, stops crying. The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sutra, Fascicle Twenty, says: “Just as when a baby cries, the parents speak to it with a yellow poplar leaf, saying: ‘Don’t cry! Don’t cry! I will give you gold.’ The baby, seeing it, forms the notion of real gold and stops crying — yet that poplar leaf is not gold at all.”

In the above kōans, three levels are spoken of: “The mind is the Buddha,” “Not mind, not Buddha,” and “Not mind, not Buddha, not a thing.” The mind spoken of here refers to self-nature. “The mind is the Buddha” means the Buddha is nothing other than this: the perfectly awakened self-nature is the Buddha. “Not mind, not Buddha” means self-nature and Buddha are both illusions, matters within the dream of ignorance. “Not mind, not Buddha, not a thing” speaks of “that one” who dreams the dream of ignorance.
Q:
All sentient beings have always been Buddhas; since they are Buddhas, why do they arise in ignorance and fall to the state of sentient beings?

A: All sentient beings originally possess the wisdom and marks of the Tathāgata, so they are said to “have always been Buddhas”; but there is still fundamental ignorance in a dormant state. Once it manifests its activity (a single thought of unawareness) and enters the dream of ignorance, one falls to the state of sentient beings. The process is: a single thought of unawareness gives rise to the three subtle marks, and the realm of objects is the support for the arising of the six coarse marks. (See
The Mind, Self-Nature, and the Tathāgatagarbha
Q: If ignorance has always existed, then since there is ignorance, how can it be said that one has become a Buddha?

A: Although the primordial Buddha has fundamental ignorance, it is in a dormant state, so one still possesses the wisdom and marks of the Tathāgata. Since one possesses the wisdom and marks of the Tathāgata, one is of course a Buddha.

Q: All sentient beings have already become Buddhas, and afterward arose in ignorance, entered the dream of ignorance, and fell to the state of sentient beings. So when we now practice, after we become Buddhas, at what time will we again arise in ignorance, enter the dream of ignorance, and fall to the state of sentient beings?

A: Our present practice to become a Buddha is precisely to eradicate fundamental ignorance. So, having eradicated fundamental ignorance and become a Buddha, one will not again arise in ignorance, enter the dream of ignorance, and fall to the state of sentient beings. This is like a person who, before having smallpox, is a healthy person; having caught smallpox he becomes a patient; after recovery he is a healthy person again, and has lifelong immunity, never again catching smallpox. With regard to this, in the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment the Buddha taught: “Good man! Like smelting gold ore, the gold does not come into being because of the smelting; once it has been smelted into pure gold, it will never again become ore.

The Tathāgata’s perfect awakening is likewise.” (Translation: Good man! Like refining gold ore, the gold does not exist because of the refining; since it has already been refined into pure gold, it will never again become ore.
The Tathāgata’s perfect awakening is also thus (it does not reverse).)

[Fundamental ignorance] From the beginningless beginning, a single thought of unawareness enters the dream of ignorance, and through the long night of delusion, not knowing the truth, it is able to give rise to all delusions and afflictions; this is called fundamental ignorance, also called beginningless ignorance. The Sutra on the Principle of the Six Pāramitās of the Great Vehicle says: “The fierce flame of wind-blown fire can be controlled, and the waves of the sea can also be stilled; only the delusive mind is very hard to tame. Why? Because from the beginningless beginning, ignorance deludes the nature of the mind.”
Regarding the summary of the Sutra on the Buddha’s Treasury, Master Ouyi’s Guide to the Knowledge of the Canon says:

Chapter One: The Real Nature of All Dharmas. For Śāriputra he spoke the ten similes such as painting in empty space, to show that the Tathāgata speaks of all dharmas as neither arising nor ceasing, without mark and without doing, causing people to believe and understand — this is all the more rare.
Chapter Two: Buddha-Recitation. It clarifies that to be without discrimination, without grasping and without abandoning, is true Buddha-recitation.

Chapter Three: Recitation of the Dharma, Chapter Four: Recitation of the Saṅgha, Chapter Five: Pure Precepts. It clarifies that precept-breaking bhikṣus complete the ten arrows of sorrow and affliction and must fall into evil destinies.

Chapter Six: Pure Dharma. It clarifies that Kāśyapa Buddha predicted that in the Dharma of Śākyamuni many would receive offerings, so the Dharma should quickly be extinguished, like the blind being deceived by thieves and falling into a deep pit.

Chapter Seven: The Past. It clarifies that after the Buddha of Great Adornment passed into extinction, the assembly divided into five groups; the one who understood the true Dharma is now Pūrṇa (Fulouzi), while the four who spoke false Dharma long fell into hell, and now have emerged as Devadatta and the others.

Chapter Eight: Pure Views. It clarifies that Śākyamuni, in the past, successively attended many Buddhas; because of his attachment to attainment, he did not receive a prediction, until at the time of the Buddha Dīpaṃkara he awakened to the endurance of non-arising and then received the prediction.

“Chapter Nine: The Precepts Explained. It clarifies that three kinds of people do not delight in hearing this sutra: first, those who break the precepts; second, those of overweening pride; third, those who teach the Dharma impurely and those who cling to a self. Next it clarifies that a single division of the light-mark of the white curl is able to supply bhikṣus who practice the Dharma according to the Dharma, so that the bhikṣu need not worry about the four requisites (robe, food, bedding, and medicine) but should only single-mindedly pursue the path.

Chapter Ten: The Entrustment. It fully clarifies the unwholesome affairs of the latter age, and the entrustment being completed. Māra was grieved and wept, because the Buddha had foreseen and guarded against it, so that he could not destroy the true Dharma. The Buddha further spoke a verse to conclude the preceding meaning.”

blocks.text: Chapter One: The Real Nature of All Dharmas

inline.s: In this chapter, the World-Honored One used the ten similes such as painting in empty space to show that the real nature of all dharmas (all dharmas neither arise nor cease, without mark and without doing) causes people to believe and understand — this is all the more rare. Then, in detail, he reveals the real nature of all dharmas: all dharmas are ultimately empty, non-existent, and unobtainable.
[Neither arising nor ceasing] All dharmas never existed (originally never arose, therefore also never cease). Therefore all things are illusions.

[Thus have I heard. At one time the Buddha dwelt on Vulture Peak in Rājagṛha, together with a great assembly of bhikṣus, all well known, and the limitless, countless hosts of great bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.]

This is what I (Ānanda) personally heard and saw. At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha dwelt on Vulture Peak in Rājagṛha, together with the great assembly of bhikṣus, all of them well known, as well as the boundless hosts of great bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, immeasurable and countless.

[At that time, Śāriputra rose from samādhi, went to the Buddha, bared his right shoulder, bowed his head at the Buddha’s feet, and said to the Buddha: Rare! World-Honored One, what the Tathāgata speaks — that all dharmas neither arise nor cease, without mark and without doing — causes people to believe and understand. The Buddha told Śāriputra: What benefit do you see that you exclaim ‘rare,’ that what the Tathāgata speaks — that all dharmas neither arise nor cease, without mark and without doing — causes people to believe and understand?]

At that time, Śāriputra rose from samādhi, came before the Buddha, bared his right shoulder, knelt on his right knee, joined his palms in reverence, and said to the Buddha: Rare! World-Honored One, what you proclaim — that all dharmas neither arise nor cease, without mark and without doing — can cause people to believe and understand. The Buddha said to Śāriputra: What benefit do you see that you exclaim that what the Tathāgata speaks, that all dharmas neither arise nor cease, without mark and without doing, causes people to believe and understand, is rare?

[Samādhi] Also called sammatti or samata; in Chinese it is translated “concentration” (ding), meaning the mind fixed on one point. When a practitioner’s six faculties contact the realm of the six objects outside, if one can refrain from giving rise to mind, from being moved by thoughts, from discriminating, and from clinging, this is called “concentration,” which is entering the state of “samādhi.” [Rare] Incomparably supreme, rare and difficult to encounter. [All dharmas neither arise nor cease, without mark and without doing] All dharmas are like matters in a dream; in reality they originally never arose, so they also never cease; originally never arose, so they have no form or mark; originally never arose, so there is no doing — this is the real nature of all dharmas. Therefore the real nature of all dharmas is the Dharma of non-arising. Sentient beings, deluded, see only arising and ceasing within the serene non-arising; the Buddhas, awakened, see only non-arising within the apparent arising and ceasing.

[Śāriputra said to the Buddha: World-Honored One, in a quiet place I constantly reflect thus: the World-Honored One speaks of the dharmas without name and mark by means of name and mark, and the Dharma without words by means of words; pondering this, I gave rise to a rare mind. The Buddha told Śāriputra: So it is, so it is. This matter is rare, the first and rarest — namely, that the Buddhas’ anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi is this.]

Śāriputra replied: World-Honored One, in a quiet place I constantly reflect: the World-Honored One speaks of the dharmas without name and mark by means of name and mark, and the Dharma without words by means of words; therefore I gave rise to a rare mind. The Buddha said to Śāriputra: So it is, so it is. This matter (clarifying with name and mark and words the real nature of all dharmas, which is apart from name and mark and apart from words) is rare, the first and rarest — for the real nature of all dharmas, in which nothing arises or ceases, without mark and without doing, is precisely the unsurpassed right and perfect enlightenment of all Buddhas!

[Name and mark] Terms and phrases. [Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi] The name of the Buddha’s wisdom; in Chinese it is translated “unsurpassed right and perfect enlightenment.” The Great Perfection of Wisdom Treatise says: “Only a single person, the Buddha, has wisdom that is anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”

[Śāriputra, it is like a skillful painter painting various colors in empty space. What do you think, is this painter rare? Rare, World-Honored One. Śāriputra, that the Tathāgata, having attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, speaks of all dharmas as neither arising nor ceasing, without mark and without doing, and causes people to believe and understand — this is all the more rare!]

Śāriputra, it is like a very skillful painter who is able to paint various pictures in empty space. What do you think? Is this painter rare? Śāriputra replied: Rare! World-Honored One. The World-Honored One said: Śāriputra, that the Tathāgata, with the unsurpassed right and perfect enlightenment he has attained, speaks of all dharmas as neither arising nor ceasing, without mark and without doing, and causes people to believe and understand — this is doubly rare!

This simile, of a skillful painter painting in empty space, reveals that when the Buddha speaks of the real nature of all dharmas (all dharmas neither arise nor cease, without mark and without doing) and causes people to believe and understand, it is the first and rarest thing! One cannot paint in empty space; yet there is a skillful painter who paints in empty space, which is very rare; and the Buddha, with unsurpassed wisdom, speaks of all dharmas as neither arising nor ceasing, without mark and without doing, causing people to believe and understand — this is doubly rare!

[Why? Because it is the Dharma without name and mark, without thought or attainment, and also without cultivation, inconceivable, not a support of mind, without idle talk, not something on which idle talk can rest, without thinking or observing, having nothing held, not abiding in mind, no attainment of the attained, without this or that, without discrimination, without movement and without nature, originally self-empty, not thinkable and not to be gotten out of — all the world cannot believe it. Such is the Dharma without name and mark, spoken by means of name and mark. Thus, Śāriputra, that all dharmas neither arise nor cease, without mark and without doing, causes people to believe and understand — this is all the more rare!]

Why? Because this is the Dharma without name and mark, without thought or attainment, and also without cultivation, inconceivable, not a support of mind, without idle talk, not something on which idle talk can rest, without thinking or observing, having nothing held, not abiding in mind, no attainment of the attained, without this or that, without discrimination, without movement and without nature, originally self-empty, not thinkable and not to be gotten out of — all the world cannot believe it. Such a Dharma without name and mark is spoken by means of name and mark. Therefore, Śāriputra, to speak of all dharmas as neither arising nor ceasing, without mark and without doing, and to cause people to believe and understand — this is doubly rare!

[Name and mark] The technical terms of Buddhism are called “name and mark.” [The Dharma without name and mark] Name-and-mark are the names of things, but all dharmas do not exist at all, so the various names and marks are only fictitious designations, called “provisional names.” [Provisional name] Dharmas are originally nameless; this is an artificial imposition of man. Therefore all names are false and untrue, not corresponding to a real entity, like giving a poor and lowly person the name of wealth and nobility — such is a provisional name. The Exposition of the Meaning of the Great Vehicle says: “Dharmas are nameless; provisionally a name is imposed, hence called a provisional name, as a poor person is provisionally called wealthy and noble.” [Idle talk] Unrealistic talk. [Thinking and observing] The newer translation is “initial application and sustained application,” the older translation is “thinking and observing.” Coarse thought is called thinking, subtle thought is called observing; both disturb the concentrated mind.

This chapter altogether raises ten similes to reveal that when the Buddha speaks of the real nature of all dharmas (all dharmas neither arise nor cease, without mark and without doing) and causes people to believe and understand, it is the first and rarest thing! The above is the first simile, so it is spoken at length; the following nine similes are spoken briefly.

[Śāriputra, it is like a person chewing and swallowing Mount Sumeru and causing it entirely to disappear, and flying through empty space without any trouble. What do you think, is this rare? Rare, World-Honored One. Śāriputra, that the Buddhas speak of all dharmas as neither arising nor ceasing, without mark and without doing, and cause people to believe and understand — this is all the more rare!]

Śāriputra, it is like a person who can chew and swallow Mount Sumeru into his belly, and easily fly through the air. What do you think? Is this rare? Śāriputra replied: Rare! World-Honored One. The World-Honored One said: Śāriputra, that the Buddhas speak of all dharmas as neither arising nor ceasing, without mark and without doing, and cause people to believe and understand — this is doubly rare!

[Sumeru] That is, Mount Sumeru, the center of a small world. In Chinese it is translated “Sublime High Mountain.” This mountain is made of the four treasures of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal, hence it is called “sublime”; no mountain can match its height, hence it is called “high.”

[Śāriputra, it is like a city of fire, square and deep, each side one yojana, flames issuing from four gates. A man carrying dry grass passes through it; a violent wind blows up the flames and burns and bursts his body. This man is able to keep the fire from burning the grass and from burning his body, emerging from it unharmed. What do you think, is this rare? Rare, World-Honored One. Śāriputra, that the Tathāgata speaks of all dharmas as neither arising nor ceasing, without mark and without doing, and causes people to believe and understand — this is all the more rare!]

Śāriputra, it is like a city of fire, square and deep, each side one yojana, with all four city gates raging with fire. Someone carrying dry grass passes through it, and a violent wind blows the fierce fire to burn him. And this man is able to keep the great fire from burning either the grass or his body, and safely emerges from the fierce fire without a hair’s damage. What do you think? Is this rare? Śāriputra replied: Rare! World-Honored One. The World-Honored One said: Śāriputra, that the Tathāgata speaks of all dharmas as neither arising nor ceasing, without mark and without doing, and causes people to believe and understand — this is doubly rare!
[Yojana] An Indian unit of distance. There are three kinds: the great yojana is about eighty li, the medium yojana about sixty li, the small yojana about forty li.

[Śāriputra, it is like a person using rock as a raft, crossing from this shore of the sea to the other shore. What do you think, is this rare? Rare, World-Honored One. Śāriputra, that the Tathāgata speaks of all dharmas as neither arising nor ceasing, without mark and without doing, and causes people to believe and understand — this is all the more rare!]

Śāriputra, it is like a person using rock as a raft, crossing from this shore of the great sea to the other shore. What do you think? Is this rare? Śāriputra replied: Rare! World-Honored One. The World-Honored One said: Śāriputra, that the Tathāgata speaks of all dharmas as neither arising nor ceasing, without mark and without doing, and causes people to believe and understand — this is doubly rare!

[Śāriputra, it is like a person carrying on his back the four continents and all the mountains, rivers, grass, and trees of Mount Sumeru, and using a mosquito’s leg as a ladder to climb to the Brahmā heaven. What do you think, is this rare? Rare, World-Honored One. Śāriputra, that the Tathāgata speaks of all dharmas as neither arising nor ceasing, without mark and without doing, and causes people to believe and understand — this is all the more rare!]

Śāriputra, it is like a person carrying on his back the four great continents and all the mountains, rivers, grass, and trees of Mount Sumeru, and using a mosquito’s leg as a ladder to climb to the Brahmā heaven. What do you think? Is this rare? Śāriputra replied: Rare! World-Honored One. The World-Honored One said: Śāriputra, that the Tathāgata speaks of all dharmas as neither arising nor ceasing, without mark and without doing, and causes people to believe and understand — this is doubly rare!

[The four continents] The four great continents to the east, south, west, and north of Mount Sumeru: Pūrvavideha (so named because its inhabitants’ forms excel), Jambudvīpa (also called Yānfuti), Aparagodānīya, and Uttarakuru. [And Mount Sumeru] And Mount Sumeru. The “zhu” here is a contraction of “zhi yu” or “zhi hu.” For example, in the story of The Foolish Old Man Who Moved the Mountains: “Throwing it to the end of the Bohai Sea.” [The Brahmā heaven] The first dhyāna heaven of the realm of form.

[Śāriputra, it is like a lotus thread hanging Mount Sumeru in empty space. What do you think, is this rare? Rare, World-Honored One. Śāriputra, that the Tathāgata speaks of all dharmas as neither arising nor ceasing, without mark and without doing, and causes people to believe and understand — this is all the more rare!]

Śāriputra, it is like hanging Mount Sumeru in empty space with a lotus thread. What do you think? Is this rare? Śāriputra replied: Rare! World-Honored One. The World-Honored One said: Śāriputra, that the Tathāgata speaks of all dharmas as neither arising nor ceasing, without mark and without doing, and causes people to believe and understand — this is doubly rare!

[Śāriputra, it is like when the great fire of the kalpa-end burns, a person with a single spittle can extinguish this fire, and with a single breath again form a world and its various heavenly palaces. What do you think, is this rare? Rare, World-Honored One. Śāriputra, that the Tathāgata speaks of all dharmas as neither arising nor ceasing, without mark and without doing, and causes people to believe and understand — this is all the more rare!]

Śāriputra, it is like when the kalpa-fire burns, a person can, with a single mouthful of spittle, extinguish this fire, and with a single breath restore the worlds and heavenly palaces that have been burned to ashes. What do you think? Is this rare? Śāriputra replied: Rare! World-Honored One. The World-Honored One said: Śāriputra, that the Tathāgata speaks of all dharmas as neither arising nor ceasing, without mark and without doing, and causes people to believe and understand — this is doubly rare!

[Kalpa-fire] The great fire that occurs at the time of the kalpa of destruction, burning up to the first dhyāna heaven, turning everything to ashes. [The kalpa of destruction] A great kalpa contains four intermediate kalpas: formation, abiding, destruction, and emptiness. At the end of the kalpa of destruction, fire, water, and wind calamities must arise.

[Śāriputra, is the Ganges great and immeasurable? So it is, World-Honored One. Śāriputra, if throughout the four continents a great rain fell, each raindrop like the Ganges, and a person caught all these raindrops in his hand without letting any fall. What do you think, is this rare? Rare, World-Honored One. Śāriputra, that the Tathāgata speaks of all dharmas as neither arising nor ceasing, without mark and without doing, and causes people to believe and understand — this is all the more rare!]

Śāriputra, is the water of the Ganges great and immeasurable? Śāriputra replied: So it is, World-Honored One. The World-Honored One said: Śāriputra, if throughout the four continents a great rain fell, and each raindrop were as great and immeasurable as the water of the Ganges, and a person caught all these raindrops in his hand without omitting any. What do you think? Is this rare? Śāriputra replied: Rare! World-Honored One. The World-Honored One said: Śāriputra, that the Tathāgata speaks of all dharmas as neither arising nor ceasing, without mark and without doing, and causes people to believe and understand — this is doubly rare!
[Raindrops like the Ganges] The raindrops are as great and immeasurable as the water of the Ganges. “Di” (di) is an old form of “di” (drop).

[Śāriputra, is Sumeru, king of mountains, high and great? High and great, World-Honored One. Śāriputra, if throughout the four continents great stones rained down, each like Mount Sumeru, and a person caught these stones in his hand without letting fall one as small as a mustard seed. What do you think, is this rare? Rare, World-Honored One. Śāriputra, that the Tathāgata speaks of all dharmas as neither arising nor ceasing, without mark and without doing, and causes people to believe and understand — this is all the more rare!]

Śāriputra, is Sumeru, king of mountains, very high and great? Śāriputra replied: Very high and great, World-Honored One. The World-Honored One said: Śāriputra, if throughout the four continents great stones rained down like rain, each stone as huge as Mount Sumeru, and a person caught all these stones in his hand without letting fall any, as though catching mustard seeds. What do you think? Is this rare? Śāriputra replied: Rare! World-Honored One. The World-Honored One said: Śāriputra, that the Tathāgata speaks of all dharmas as neither arising nor ceasing, without mark and without doing, and causes people to believe and understand — this is doubly rare!

[Śāriputra, it is like a person placing all sentient beings in his left hand, while his right hand lifts up the mountains, rivers, grass, and trees of the three thousand great-thousand world, and is able to cause all those sentient beings in his left hand to be of the same mind rejoicing, with no difference of mind. What do you think, is this rare? Rare, World-Honored One. Śāriputra, that the Tathāgata speaks of all dharmas as neither arising nor ceasing, without mark and without doing, and causes people to believe and understand — this is all the more rare!]

Śāriputra, it is like a person placing all sentient beings in his left hand, while his right hand lifts up the mountains, rivers, grass, and trees of the three thousand great-thousand world, and is able to cause all those sentient beings in his left hand to be of exactly the same mind, rejoicing in the mountains, rivers, grass, and trees in his right hand. What do you think? Is this rare? Śāriputra replied: Rare! World-Honored One. The World-Honored One said: Śāriputra, that the Tathāgata speaks of all dharmas as neither arising nor ceasing, without mark and without doing, and causes people to believe and understand — this is doubly rare!

[The three thousand great-thousand world] That is, one great-thousand world, the realm of a single Buddha’s teaching. One Mount Sumeru together with the four great continents is called a small world; a thousand small worlds form a “small chiliocosm”; a thousand small chiliocosms form a “medium chiliocosm”; a thousand medium chiliocosms form a “great chiliocosm.” Because it is three times multiplied by a thousand, a great chiliocosm is also called the “three-thousand great-thousand world.”

Above, the World-Honored One raised ten similes in succession to portray how difficult it is to “speak of the real nature of all dharmas and cause people to believe and understand.” Below, the World-Honored One specifically speaks the real nature of all dharmas — all dharmas are ultimately empty, non-existent, and unobtainable.

[Śāriputra, the dharmas spoken by the Tathāgata have no nature, are empty and non-existent, and are hard for all the world to believe and understand. Why? Śāriputra, this Dharma is without thought, apart from all thoughts; without reflection, apart from all reflections; without grasping or abandoning; without idle talk and without vexation and heat; not this shore, not the other shore, not dry land; not delusion and not clarity. Only by immeasurable wisdom can it be understood, not by what thinking can know.]

Śāriputra, the dharmas spoken by the Tathāgata have no real substance (no nature), are empty and non-existent, and this is what all the world finds hard to believe and understand. Why? Śāriputra, because this sage Dharma (dharmas without nature, empty and non-existent) is without thought, apart from all thoughts; without reflection, apart from all reflections; without grasping or abandoning; without idle talk and without vexation and heat; not this shore, not the other shore, not dry land; not delusion and not clarity. Only by immeasurable wisdom can it be understood, not by what thinking can know.

[All dharmas without nature, empty and non-existent] All dharmas have no real substance and are all illusions (like matters in a dream), truly non-existent. Here “nature” means real substance. [This Dharma] That is, the “sage Dharma” spoken of below. [Not this shore, not the other shore, not dry land] This shore is a metaphor for birth-and-death, the other shore for nirvāṇa. Dry land is the island between the two shores, a metaphor for the “eternal existence” spoken of by outsiders.
The World-Honored One further reveals “all dharmas without nature, empty and non-existent”:

[Without practice and without mark, without vexation and heat; without thought, passing beyond all thoughts; without mind, passing beyond all minds; without facing toward or away; without bondage or liberation; without delusion and without a Dharma of delusion; without ignorance and without a Dharma of ignorance; without the net of ignorance; without name and without speech; without speaking and without not-speaking; without end and without not-end; without practice and without practice-mark; without the path and without the fruit of the path; without separation, passing beyond all separations; without reflection and without mixing; not grasping, not abandoning; without attainment and not to be attained; removing all obstructions and clingings; removing greed, anger, and ignorance; not real and not false; not eternal and not impermanent; not clear and not unclear; not dark and not illumining; not abiding in mind, having no nature, its nature originally empty.]

This sage Dharma (all dharmas without nature, empty and non-existent) is without practice and without mark, without vexation and heat; without thought, passing beyond all thoughts; without mind, passing beyond all minds; without facing toward or away; without bondage or liberation; without delusion and without a Dharma of delusion; without ignorance and without a Dharma of ignorance; without the net of doubt; without name and without speech; without speaking and without not-speaking; without end and without not-end; without practice and without practice-mark; without the Dharma of the path and without the fruit of the path; without separation, passing beyond all separations; without reflection and without mixing; not grasping, not abandoning; without attainment and without non-attainment; removing all obstructions and clingings; removing greed, anger, and ignorance; not real and not false; not eternal and not impermanent; not clear and not unclear; not dark and not illumining; not abiding in mind, without real substance (having no nature), its essence being empty and non-existent (its nature originally empty).

Because everything is a matter within the dream of ignorance, whatever it is, it is “without” and “not.” The World-Honored One used many “without” and “not” to further reveal the truth of the real nature of all dharmas — “originally not a single thing” — that all dharmas are ultimately empty, non-existent, and unobtainable.

[There is no net of ignorance] Some versions have “there is no net of doubt.” [Without the path and without the fruit of the path] Without the Dharma of the path and without the fruit of the path. The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sutra

Chapter on Practice and Response, Chapter Three, says: “No stream-entry, no fruit of stream-entry, no once-returner, no fruit of once-returner, no non-returner, no fruit of non-returner, no arhat, no fruit of arhat, no pratyekabuddha, no path of the pratyekabuddha; no Buddha, and no Buddha path.” [Mixing] Mingling and blending together.
The World-Honored One reveals the function of this sage Dharma — “all dharmas without nature, empty and non-existent”:

[It can subdue Māra, subdue afflictions, subdue the five aggregates, subdue the twelve sense-fields, subdue the eighteen realms; subdue those who speak of the five aggregates, subdue those who speak of the twelve sense-fields, subdue those who speak of the eighteen realms; subdue those who speak of a sentient being, speak of a person, speak of a life, speak of a soul, speak of existence, speak of non-existence; subdue all the practitioners of wrong paths. Śāriputra, this sage Dharma of mine is able to subdue all greed and clinging, those who speak of a Dharma of existence, those who do not believe and delight in the real nature of all dharmas, and those who go against the Buddha’s Dharma.]
